title: Juniper and the Postcard
premise: Yara Underhill, a single mother and owner of the town's failing bookshop, joins the library's anonymous pen-pal program to drum up community goodwill — only to discover her assigned correspondent is Elias Vane, the developer whose company is buying out Main Street, including her lease. Their letters, written without names at first, become the one place both can be honest; when identities are revealed mid-negotiation, Yara must choose between exposing a document that could save her shop but destroy Elias's career, or protecting the man she has come to love. In the end, Yara publishes the truth anyway — and Elias, choosing loyalty to her over loyalty to his corrupt firm, testifies against his own board. The bookshop survives as a co-op, the bakery lease passes to Yara's neighbor, and Elias stays in Juniper past the last train, rebuilding from nothing beside her.
about_author: Rosalind Hartwell is a former small-town librarian who spent a decade cataloguing other people's love stories before writing her own. She lives above a bookshop not unlike Yara's, where she still answers every letter by hand.

chapters.title: The Last Train Schedule
chapters.summary: Yara's POV. Twelve years after fleeing a life that burned down, Yara counts her blessings in small safe increments: a daughter, a bookshop, a lease with eight months left. The library announces an anonymous pen-pal program to boost winter foot traffic, and Yara signs up for goodwill. Beat: cautious hope shadowed by old fear of trusting anything big.

chapters.title: Dear Stranger
chapters.summary: Elias's POV. Elias Vane, in town to finalize the Meridian Group's acquisition of Main Street properties, signs up for the pen-pal program on a whim to escape board calls. His first letter to 'Stranger No. 14' is flippant; her reply eviscerates him charmingly. He writes back honestly for the first time in years. Beat: unexpected delight, the crack in his armor.

chapters.title: What the Letters Don't Say
chapters.summary: Alternating POV. Over six weeks the letters deepen — Yara confesses her fear of beginnings; Elias admits he builds things he doesn't believe in. In person, they clash publicly over the development at a town meeting, each unknowingly sharpening the wit the other falls for on paper. Beat: dramatic irony tightening; readers see what they cannot.

chapters.title: Postmarked Juniper
chapters.summary: Yara's POV. A misdelivered postcard reveals her correspondent lives in Juniper. Yara, half in love with a stranger, begins hunting clues while Elias realizes with dawning horror who No. 14 must be — the bookseller whose lease he's scheduled to terminate. Beat: yearning curdling into dread as the reveal approaches.

chapters.title: The Reveal
chapters.summary: Dual POV. The library's unmasking party forces the truth: enemies, matched. Public humiliation for both. Yara burns the letters; Elias, unable to stop, leaves one more on her doorstep — an apology that admits the acquisition targets her block specifically. Beat: heartbreak, but the door left deliberately unlocked.

chapters.title: Terms of Surrender
chapters.summary: Elias's POV. Elias stalls the demolition timeline from inside, buying Yara months, and offers her a relocation package she refuses. Searching Meridian files for leverage, he finds evidence the firm falsified environmental surveys for the whole street. Beat: loyalty to his company fractures against loyalty to truth — and to her.

chapters.title: The Document
chapters.summary: Yara's POV. Elias shows Yara the falsified surveys: proof that could kill the project and save her shop, but releasing it ends his career and exposes him to litigation. He asks her to decide. Yara, who once lost everything to another man's secrets, refuses to be complicit in silence again. Beat: the thematic crux — power, truth, and what love may cost.

chapters.title: Everything Burns Twice
chapters.summary: Yara's POV. Yara gives the documents to the town council and a journalist; the story detonates. Meridian suspends Elias pending investigation; the town turns on Yara for 'betraying' the jobs the project promised. Her daughter asks why truth matters if it hurts people. Beat: isolation, the lowest point, memory of her first ruin echoing.

chapters.title: Testimony
chapters.summary: Elias's POV. At the state hearing, Elias chooses: he testifies against his own board, corroborating everything, surrendering his severance and reputation. Walking out, he finds Yara waiting — not to thank him, but to ask if he'd do it again knowing he'd lose. Yes, he says. Beat: climax resolved through character, not plot convenience.

chapters.title: After the Last Train
chapters.summary: Alternating POV. Spring: the bookshop becomes a community co-op; the bakery lease passes to Yara's neighbor; Meridian's project dies in committee. Elias, jobless and staying in a rented room above the bakery, asks to stay past the last train — permanently. Yara, who measured life in safe steps, takes one large one. Beat: earned resolution; love built on truth, not comfort.
